analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal was introduced in 1995 with 8 cosponsors, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 1039 would have wiped three taxes off the books: the estate tax on large inheritances, the gift tax on large transfers between living people, and the tax on transfers that skip a generation (like a grandparent leaving money straight to a grandchild). The money those taxes raise would be gone, so either other taxes go up, the deficit grows, or government programs get cut. The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. In 1995 only estates worth more than $600,000 owed the estate tax at all, so repeal would be a direct windfall to the families with the biggest fortunes. Repealing the gift tax would also let wealthy people hand over money during their lifetime with no tax, and repealing the generation-skipping tax would let fortunes pass to grandchildren untaxed. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Families inheriting estates above the taxable threshold would pay nothing: the bill repeals chapter 11 of the tax code, the estate tax, for all deaths after enactment. [S3]
Wealthy people could give away money during their lives tax-free, since the bill repeals the gift tax (chapter 12) for transfers after enactment. [S3]

Fortunes could pass from one generation to a younger one, such as grandparent to grandchild, without the extra layer of tax, since the bill repeals chapter 13, the generation-skipping transfer tax. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers as a whole. The estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes raise billions of dollars a year; repealing all three would permanently shrink federal revenue, which must be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or cuts to spending. The savings, meanwhile, would go almost entirely to a small number of very wealthy heirs. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The repeal would permanently cut federal revenue, forcing other taxes up, adding to the deficit, or forcing program cuts — costs spread across everyone, while the gains go only to heirs of large estates. [S2] [S3]

Repealing the gift tax at the same time as the estate tax would open a route to move money out of an estate entirely during life, so very wealthy families could avoid transfer taxes in all forms. [S3]

The good-faith case for the bill: supporters argue the estate tax taxes money that was already taxed when it was earned, and that it can force grieving families to sell a farm or a small business to pay the bill. Repeal would end those problems, though the benefit still flows overwhelmingly to the largest estates, since smaller ones fall under the exemption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concentrated: a tax cut worth the most to the largest inheritances. The costs are diffuse: billions in lost annual revenue borne by every federal taxpayer. There is no mechanism in the bill to make up the lost money, so on its own terms it is a straightforward transfer of tax burden from wealthy heirs to everyone else, softened only by the argument that the estate tax is a second tax on already-taxed savings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee — never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote — until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 and the bill died.

narrative.text: Philip Crane introduced the bill on February 24, 1995, with original cosponsors including Reps. Blute, McKeon, and Hancock. [S3]
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day. [S5]
Eight Republicans signed on as cosponsors, but the committee took no further action, and no vote ever happened before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997. [S4] [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off because the bill died: the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes stayed on the books, and their revenue was not shifted onto everyone else. Wealthy families who would have paid those taxes lost the chance at the windfall.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; wealthy heirs lost their windfall

for.name: Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes on February 24, 1995.

for.name: 8 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal, adding their names in support.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Bill Archer (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican, but no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: In 1995 only estates above roughly $600,000 owed any estate tax, so repeal would have been worth the most to the biggest fortunes — potentially millions per family — while the lost revenue would be spread across all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning, trust, and tax advisory services
industries.note: Lawyers, accountants, and trust companies earn fees helping clients structure estates around these taxes; full repeal would shrink that business. The effect is real but modest compared with the direct stakes of estate owners.
